data.title: Anthropic's Share Count May Be Even Higher, Columbia Prof Says — WSJ
data.description:
By Telis Demos

Counting Anthropic's shares isn't simple. The basic count and the fully diluted count results in market values that differ by hundreds of billions of dollars.

Some investors and analysts have been using a fully diluted count outlined in the prospectus. That count, around 18 billion, is billions more shares than the roughly 13 billion basic tally-or in market value terms, about $1.6 trillion versus $1.2 trillion at recent share prices.

But according to Columbia Business School auditing and accounting professor Shivaram Rajgopal, there is a case to be made for using an even larger sharecount figure.

Rajgopal, in a post this week, writes that his count of "everything that can plausibly turn into stock" is around 21 billion shares. The analysis was based on a $97 share price, roughly Thursday's close of $97.17.

His expanded count included several adjustments, such as potential further issuance to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund over the next decade, plus shares reserved for employee donation matching beyond what is already tied to vested equity, as well as shares that could be issued to settle some $67 billion of financing from Amazon, Google and Broadcom.

Rajgopal writes that when calculating earnings per share, or EPS, "there is no single right S for Anthropic. The fairer approach is to show the range and say which S you are using."

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: AI tech rout prompts US investors to rush into value stocks
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nasdaq now down almost 2% year to date, was up 19% YTD in October
  • More Fed rate hikes seen pressuring growth stocks near term
  • Median S&P 500 stock up 7% in 2026, index up only 2% so far

By Noel Randewich, Caroline Valetkevitch and Sinéad Carew

putting down for a tweak -dg

Wall Street fled headlong on Friday from the AI boom to the relative safety of bonds and lower-priced shares outside the tech sector.

Technology carnage was extensive. Anthropic’s sharp decline took it within a whisker of its IPO price before recovering to trade down 10%, just a day after a record debut that briefly valued the AI lab above $2 trillion. The Nasdaq composite was down over 4% for its third decline of 2% or more this week, its biggest weekly decline since last year’s Liberation Day rout. The pullback put it lower for the year for the first time since April.

The Nasdaq is now down almost 2% in 2026, relinquishing an annual gain of almost 19% through early October.

The retreat partly reflects expectations that high inflation readings will force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in coming months, likely further increasing borrowing costs and compressing valuations – and making Treasuries and so-called value stocks look like a better bet.

“Yesterday’s AI IPO is a valuation test, and with the 10-year around 5% and the Fed still hiking, investors are asking how much of the AI story is already priced in,” said Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera, El Segundo, California.

Friday’s action highlights the shift in fortunes on Wall Street since the Nasdaq hit its last high on October 6. A handful of AI-related heavyweights had accounted for most of the S&P 500’s gains for much of 2026, masking underwhelming returns from the index’s other components.

But the median S&P 500 CBOE:SPX stock now is up almost 7% in 2026. That beats the 2% year-to-date gain in the S&P 500, which has been hobbled of late by a 46% slump in Nvidia and deep declines in other AI stocks, including a 12% drop in Broadcom on Friday.

The rotation away from tech is making winners out of a sector that has long been overlooked: value stocks that trade at lower multiples to their earnings and net worth than the growth stocks that soared during the AI boom.

“Kevin Warsh represents a different approach to monetary policy, and that has introduced additional uncertainty regarding interest rates, inflation, and economic growth,” said Philip Palumbo, CEO of Palumbo Wealth Management. “Markets do not like uncertainty, and right now we have plenty of it.“

The S&P 500 value index is up 8% in 2026, compared to a 2% drop in the S&P 500 growth index (.IGX). The switch puts cautious value investing on track to beat growth for the first time since 2022, when inflation fears sent Wall Street into its worst slump since the 2008 financial crisis.

Many analysts and portfolio managers said they did not view the AI trade as impaired. Instead, they said, an occasional washout can improve valuations and draw in investors with a longer-term perspective.

“You have a confluence of short-term negative factors,” said Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors LLC in New York. He pointed to questions about the health of the underlying business at Nvidia , the onetime market leader whose shares have been in free fall since the Nasdaq composite hit its most recent record in October, shedding more than $2.2 trillion of market value.

“The fundamentals have not deteriorated as much as the stock prices have,” Awad said. “I would view it just as a normal violent correction in a long-term upward trend in AI spending and in the markets.”

Meanwhile, the flight to value stocks and Treasury notes, which rallied sharply on Friday, is the latest sign of markets grappling with the extent to which a slowing buildout of AI infrastructure will hit US growth – a debate that has been going on all year, if not to this extreme.

"This is your classic flight-to-safety trade. So as investors are getting a little bit more concerned about the AI trade, they're moving out of those stocks and into Treasury securities,” said Lawrence Gillum, chief fixed-income strategist at LPL Financial. “Anytime there's been some sort of hiccup in the AI trade, we've seen the Treasury market rally on the back of that."

data.title: US measles cases near 6,000 mark as outbreak worsens
data.description:
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday reported 5,838 measles cases as of November 19, as the country battles its worst outbreak of the viral infection in decades.

  • Measles cases in the US have climbed above 5,000 for the first time since 1991. Earlier this week, US lost its measles elimination status after 26 years

  • Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases including 326 hospitalizations, as of November 20

  • Wisconsin has reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated ‌death, involving a child

  • The CDC has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded

  • The gap in numbers follows a policy shift under U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., with the CDC switching to the National Center for Health Statistics' mortality data to track measles deaths, replacing its earlier reliance on state health departments' figures.

data.title: Dollar weaker as Fed-fueled rally stalls; lower US yields help yen
data.description:
Key points:
  • Dollar index still near strongest level since early April 2025
  • Falling Treasury yields support low-yielding currencies
  • Yen firms after Japanese core inflation hits 2.2%
  • Bitcoin falls below $60,000

By Saqib Iqbal Ahmed

The US dollar eased across the board on Friday as a weeks-long rally fueled by bets on a hawkish Federal Reserve lost momentum, but waning appetite for riskier currencies kept the dollar's losses in check.

The dollar index fell 0.1% to 103.86, just short of the 103.9 level it touched in the previous session, its highest since April 2025. The index was on track to snap an eight-session winning streak and is up 1.9% so far this month.

The dollar's rally accelerated on November 10, when hotter-than-expected US inflation data reinforced bets that the Fed would tighten policy and Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point hike in December should be considered.

"I think the momentum has stalled for the dollar ... but I think it's a little bit early to pick a top for the dollar," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets.

US Treasury yields dropped on Friday as a multitude of AI-related concerns weighed on global stocks and Anthropic's record market debut on Thursday did little to revive investor confidence. On Friday, investors sought out safe-haven assets. Lower Treasury yields also boosted the relative appeal of the Swiss franc. The dollar slipped 0.5% against the franc.

"When US rates are falling, low-yielding currencies look better," Chandler said.

Still, strategists see the dollar continuing to draw some support from the outlook for a hawkish Fed.

Chris Turner, global head of markets at ING, said that while there is only a weak case for another steep correction in equities, "there is no reason for the Fed to drop its hawkish rhetoric anytime soon."

He pointed to the release next week of the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, a key inflation gauge for the Fed, which Turner said will likely confirm that the US central bank needs to act.

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook on Friday made a case for more interest rate hikes, saying the US central bank's current policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels she views with "great concern."

US President Donald Trump said during a news conference on Friday that interest rates were too high because the Federal Reserve is "political."

YEN FIRMS ON INFLATION DATA

Against the yen , the dollar slipped 0.6% to 158.78, still close to levels at which Japanese authorities intervened in July to shore up the drooping currency.

"The yen has jumped today, helped by lower US rates and firm Japanese October CPI," Chandler said.

Japan's annual core inflation accelerated to 2.2% in October, staying above the central bank's 2% target for a second straight month and pointing to broadening price pressures that strengthen the case for a near-term rate hike by the Bank of Japan.

Analysts at Capital Economics argue that the yen's recent weakness is unlikely to last. With long-term inflation expectations now around target, further increases in yields would be mostly in real terms, which, combined with their view that US yields will fall, should prove yen-positive, the analysts said.

Sterling was little changed on the day but hovered near a one-year low against the dollar, at $1.3091.

Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, fell below the $60,000 level on Friday for the first time since July, as lofty valuation concerns weighed on the AI trade and other risk assets. Bitcoin was last down 6% to $57,939.

data.title: Nvidia's stock heads for a stretch of weekly losses not seen since 2008
data.description:
By Hannah Pedone

One fund manager says the continued uncertainty makes Nvidia 'vulnerable' to more selling, even as the company has erased over $900 billion in market value in the past seven days

Nvidia's stock has been sinking amid corporate tumult in recent weeks.

Nvidia's stock was on track to book a decline for the seventh week in a row - a stretch of consecutive losses not seen in nearly two decades.

A cascade of factors has left the stock (NVDA) reeling - most notably former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and its board's investigation into whether he compromised national security or revealed corporate secrets. But the stock had been under pressure even before that, with investors questioning the sustainability of artificial-intelligence demand.

Nvidia shares haven't fallen for seven weeks in a row since July 2008, when the company issued a profit warning and was working to address defects in some of its chips.

Shares of Nvidia were trading 7% lower on Friday. They've lost nearly 17% so far this week and are more than 43% from their peak close achieved in early October.

Nvidia's stock has fallen for seven days in a row, over which it has shed roughly $907 billion in market capitalization. That's more than the market value of JPMorgan Chase (JPM), which has a $835 billion market cap, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

By market value, Nvidia is now the fourth-largest U.S. company, falling below Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOGL) for the first time since April 2024, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Nvidia's market cap is now $3.28 trillion, while Alphabet's is at $3.32 trillion.

The stock's "weakness despite strong earnings shows how much it will take to restore confidence." David Miller, CIO at Catalyst Funds, told MarketWatch.

On Tuesday, Nvidia reported blockbuster earnings results and raised its revenue outlook for next year, but that wasn't enough to stem the bleeding.

Seaport Research analyst Jay Goldberg told MarketWatch that fund managers who previously held Nvidia because it was a "safety stock" are now "rotating out" amid the turmoil.

So what comes next?

Goldberg expects things to stabilize next week. "I don't think it keeps falling," he said - though adding that "there is no one in a hurry to buy it until we know who the next CEO is."

But Miller said Nvidia's stock is "vulnerable" to more selling. The length of the losing streak alone "tells us very little about where the bottom is," he told MarketWatch.

"A sharp rebound is certainly possible, but I would want greater clarity on permanent leadership and the investigations, along with continued execution on customer demand and product deliveries, before becoming confident in a sustained recovery," he said.

In a Friday news conference, President Trump said he would "like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back" to Nvidia.

"We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them," he added.

-Hannah Pedone

This content was created by MarketWatch, which is operated by Dow Jones & Co. MarketWatch is published independently from Dow Jones Newswires and The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: Ohio reports first pediatric flu death of 2026-27 season
data.description:
Ohio reported its first flu-associated pediatric death of the 2026-27 season, involving a teenager under 18 from Ross County, the state health department said on Friday.

The Ohio Department of Health said the state typically records between one and seven flu-associated pediatric deaths each season.

It added that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently rates Ohio's flu activity as low, though hospitalizations generally rise toward the end of the year.

The department urged everyone aged 6 months and older to receive an updated flu vaccine, saying vaccination can reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalization.

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

(the "Company" or "StickIt"), a developer and patent holder of proprietary cannabinoid and plant extract delivery technologies, today announces an update to it spress release of November 17, 2026 in which it announced that it will be consolidating all of the issued and outstanding common shares of the Company ("Common Shares") on the basis of one (1) post consolidation Common Share for each ​t​wo (​2) pre consolidation Common Shares (the "Consolidation").

The Corporation's board of directors previously set November 22, 2026 as the effective date of the Consolidation however this date has now been moved to November 26. data.title: CAPR Stock Gains Ahead Of Weekend FDA Deramiocel Decision After Rough Week
data.description:
Key points:
  • Company CEO Linda Marbán said earlier this month that the company's application with the FDA is in its final review stages.
  • Despite the rally on Friday, the stock is on track to clock a 17% drop this week. 
  • Earlier this month, Oppenheimer said that it sees the stock moving to $50 per share on FDA approval.

Shares of Capricor Therapeutics (CAPR) jumped 5% on Friday, despite broader market weakness, ahead of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s decision on its therapy, Deramiocel, for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), expected this weekend.

DMD is a rare, inherited genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle degeneration and weakness that presents predominantly in young boys. The company is seeking approval for deramiocel to preserve upper-limb function in patients older than nine. The FDA is slated to decide on approving Deramiocel by November 22.

Despite the rally on Friday, the stock is on track to clock a 17% drop this week.

Capricor Seeks FDA Approval With Revised Deramiocel Label

Capricor initially sought approval for cardiomyopathy associated with DMD for Deramiocel. The company’s first application was rejected in July 2025, citing a lack of substantial evidence of effectiveness. The company resubmitted the application earlier this year with HOPE-3 trial data, and the agency said it will decide on the application by August 22. However, an advisory committee met at the end of July and voted 9–3 that the evidence did not support effectiveness for cardiomyopathy.

Capricor then submitted additional 24-month clinical data analyses from the HOPE-3 trial and asked FDA to consider a refined label built on the trial’s primary endpoint—preservation of upper-limb function—rather than cardiomyopathy. The agency treated that package as a major amendment and moved the decision to November 22.

Company CEO Linda Marbán said earlier this month that the company's application with the FDA is in its final review stages. The company, in the meantime, is advancing launch preparations while pacing spending to the regulatory timeline, she said.

The management also said that it continues to pursue independent commercialization amid an ongoing arbitration with Nippon Shinyaku’s unit NS Pharma, with whom the company had initially inked a deal for distribution of the drug. Management does not expect the dispute to delay patient access if Deramiocel is approved.

Wall Street Is Divided

Earlier this month, Oppenheimer voiced optimism for approval on or around the November 22 FDA action date. The firm said that it sees the stock moving to $50 per share on FDA approval and creating a "compelling" risk/reward at current share levels.

Oppenheimer has an ‘Outperform’ rating on Capricor with a $54 price target, which implies a potential upside of about 509% from the stock’s last closing price.

H.C. Wainwright, meanwhile, said last month that it expects the FDA to reject the application, noting that it sees only a small chance of approval. The firm has a 'Neutral' rating on the stock.

How Did CAPR Retail Traders React?

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around CAPR stock stayed within the 'extremely bullish' territory at the time of writing, while message volume stayed at 'extremely high' levels.

A Stocktwits user expressed optimism for a decision announcement as early as after-hours on Friday, provided the target date falls on the weekend.

data.title: Everyone's making money off 'GTA 6' this week - except investors in Take-Two's stock
data.description:
By Bill Peters

'Grand Theft Auto VI' might be a blockbuster game, but investors are shrugging it off

"Grand Theft Auto VI" finally arrived this week.

Take-Two Interactive's "Grand Theft Auto VI" might be one of the biggest entertainment events ever, but investors haven't been impressed.

Shares of Take-Two (TTWO) - which owns Rockstar Games, the developer of "GTA 6" - are down around 8% over the past five days. While shares rallied on Wednesday, a day before the videogame's official release, they fell Thursday and then seesawed on Friday after official sales figures dropped.

Rockstar Games on Friday said first-day retail sales for the game had hit $3.79 billion. It said 32.5 million units sold pre-release.

"It's partly a sell-the-news moment," said Nick McKay, an analyst who follows the videogame industry at Freedom Capital Markets. "I think it's partly the fact that tech more broadly has been weak of late."

"GTA 6" has earned a near-perfect Metacritic score, drawing praise for its more mature storyline - a present-day Floridian twist on Bonnie and Clyde - and an immersive open-world experience. People have called in sick to spend time playing the game. Boyfriends have disappeared to tend to their in-game girlfriends. Some researchers have anticipated a spike in online food-delivery orders. Others have called the game a reflection of the garbled, unhinged state of the U.S. itself. Analysts, by and large, are optimistic about the game's prospects for years to come.

But McKay noted that "GTA 6" debuted the same week as Anthropic's (ANT) IPO, potentially steering some investors' attention away from the game. More broadly, the AI trade is a mess for multiple reasons, and AI advances, along with the cost-of-living squeeze, have posed a threat to the videogame industry.

Moreover, McKay said, investors and gamers' frustrations with Take-Two may have been building in the months leading up to the game's launch, as details about "GTA 6" remained sparse.

He said that people have been waiting for the game essentially since "Grand Theft Auto V" launched in 2013. But he said there was little news on "GTA 6" until about three months ago, when Netflix (NFLX) offered an extended look at the game in August. The game's release suffered from multiple delays. Ahead of "GTA 6's" debut, hackers also leaked footage of the game, exploiting the information vacuum, he said. Moreover, some data had shown that "NBA 2K27," which is part of Take-Two's other big videogame franchise, had underperformed.

"If we all assumed that 'GTA' would be a very well-reviewed game, and we assumed that it would perform well, you say to yourself, 'OK, well, what comes next?'" McKay said.

"We don't have really any information on when 'GTA's' going to launch on PCs, when 'GTA Online' is going to launch for the new game, so I think investors have started to look toward that," he added.

Shares of Take-Two are down 18.7% so far this year.

Oppenheimer analysts, in a note on Thursday, also suggested the game's realism was both a strength and a weakness.

"The more demanding police encounters, elaborate vehicle interactions, and everyday activities may slow gameplay and sometimes feel too laborious vs. 'GTA V,'" they said.

They also said the gameplay could be cumbersome at times. Clunky controls - for driving, fighting and other actions - "can occasionally break immersion." And they had questions over how any future online version of "GTA 6" might make money off of updates, add-ons and in-game purchases.

Morgan Stanley analysts, in a note on Thursday, said any post-launch press releases on sales figures from Take-Two could also serve as a "sell the news" event for the company's stock. Along with the launch of a PC version of the game, they, too, said investors' attention would soon shift toward how Take-Two and Rockstar can keep online players spending.

"Unlike the initial game purchase, this spending can recur over many years, as demonstrated over 'GTA Online's' 13-year history," they said. "We see the potential combination of a larger audience and higher monetization as an important driver of multi-year earnings growth, with strong launch sales establishing the foundation for the next decade of monetization."

McKay said that some Wall Street analysts who follow videogames were new to the space, and lacked historical context on how games tend to sell. Demand estimates were all over the place, and some were overly optimistic, making it difficult to please everyone, he said.

Sales for "GTA 5," he noted, spiked in the days after it hit shelves, but plateaued in the months after that initial rush. Just because an estimated 130 million to 140 million newer-generation PS5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles are in people's homes doesn't mean that many copies of "GTA 6" will be sold. And he said that few gamers were likely on the fence about whether to buy "GTA 6" at this point.

McKay pointed to other challenges for Take-Two and the rest of the industry. Shifts to digital and mobile gaming remain a threat. Consoles and other hardware are expensive. The industry's growing focus on mega-franchises - like "Grand Theft Auto" or "Call of Duty" - have threatened demand downstream. As those games gobble up more playing hours and dollars, other games can suffer, he said.

"What you see on the console side is games that would have been bigger sellers 10, 15, 20 years ago, when they launch now, the demand isn't there," he said. "Because consumers have said 'You know what? My money's going toward 'Call of Duty' now. Or, my money's going toward 'GTA.'"

-Bill Peters

data.title: Crude Oil Advances Amid Ongoing U.S.-Iran, Saudi Arabia-Houthi Hostilities
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Crude oil prices have moved higher on Friday as investors assessed the ongoing developments in the U.S.-Iran conflict as vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz continue to suffer attacks. Traders also parsed the U.S. plans to put off any decision on Iran until 2027 with cautious optimism.

WTI Crude Oil for December delivery was last seen trading up by $0.72 (or 0.87%) at $83.93 per barrel.

In an effort to tighten its naval blockade on Iran, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) warned vessels receiving Iranian cargo through ship-to-ship transfers will face military action.

On Wednesday, Iran's Navy claimed that three oil tankers caught fire as they hit naval mines while sailing east of the Strait of Hormuz after violating Iran's guidelines.

Roughly one incident per day of Iranian attacks on tankers navigating the Strait of Hormuz has been reported in November. So far this month, nearly 20 attacks occurred, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations.

Despite persisting attack threats, Persian Gulf oil exports through Hormuz and alternative route shipments from the gulf recovered to around 17.10 million barrels per day for the week through November 18 which is about 73.00% of pre-war levels of 23.30 million, according to ship tracker Kpler. The high volume has countered the upside movement for crude oil.

In its November Oil Market Report, the Paris-based International Energy Agency stated that global supply rose by 2.30 million barrels per day in October to 105.40 million bpd.

Citing a recovery in regional production and stable supplies, the agency observed that global oil supply is expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter of 2026.

This week, Energy Information Administration data added to the downward pressure after its report indicated that the U.S. commercial crude inventories rose by 3.40 million barrels to 417.80 million barrels for the week ending November 13, higher than market expectations of around 400,000 barrels.

The agency expects the global oil market to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, with a larger surplus possible in 2027.

Today, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement warned workers and people near Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports to clear out the area immediately as they are planning to hit Saudi ports in Jeddah and the Red Sea. The militant group also threatened airline services to stay out of Saudi Arabian airspace.

The Saudi-led coalition, which is fighting Yemen's Houthis stated that it intercepted five drones and one ballistic missile that targeted Riyadh.

Meanwhile, market participants assessed U.S. President Donald Trump's remarks where he stated that he will wait until 2027 on taking a decision on Iran with cautious optimism.

Speaking to Reuters, Fox News, and Axios separately, Trump clearly stated that he is not rushing to any decision on Iran and wanted to see what happens after January 1, 2027.

So far, the significance of the date is not clear. For now, traders are divided on whether Trump would stick to the timeline and not pursue any attacks on Iran.

Last week, the New York Times reported that Trump is planning for renewing attacks on Iran anytime soon, leading to concerns of fresh escalation.

Citing unnamed sources, the Axios also reported that the White House sought input from the Pentagon and intelligence experts on how Iran would respond to the strike scenarios.

According to the Baker Hughes Company's data, the U.S. crude oil rigs increased to 469 on November 20 from 463 of the previous week and total rigs increased to 607 from 601.

data.title: The Fed is too busy fighting inflation to rescue the stock market
data.description:
By Greg Robb

Concern about financial condition seems to favor a gradual pace of rate hikes

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at his press conference in October.

The U.S. stock market plunged this week into correction territory, with the major indexes down more than 10% from recent highs, but don't expect the U.S. central bank to come to the rescue.

Federal Reserve officials will continue to raise interest rates, despite the recent selloff in the stock market, as equity-market gains over the past four years dwarf the recent declines, economists said Friday.

"We would need a much larger retreat in equity values to make a dent in the wealth that has been generated by the stock market over the prior few years," said Avery Shenfeld, chief economist of CIBC Capital Markets.

Scott Anderson, chief U.S. economist at BMO Capital Markets agreed: "People have done so well over the past several years. There is some room for stocks to fall without all consumers stopping spending and air traffic going down."

Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, said most Fed officials are looking through the stock-market volatility.

"Regardless of the fact that financial conditions have tightened, they will still want to signal and implement a tighter monetary stance," Daco said.

The Fed raised rates a quarter-point in September, the first increase in three years, in an effort to battle the persistent upward creep of consumer prices.

Officials made no change to rates in October, in part because the stock market was weak, according to minutes of the Fed meeting released Wednesday. At the same time, almost all Fed officials anticipated further rate hikes.

CIBC's Shenfeld said there are two reasons why stocks would matter for the Fed: if the market falls far enough to cause negative wealth effects, or if the market is a predictor of where the economy is going.

That's less likely to be true after the huge run-up of the past few years, he said.

"At this point, I don't think it is material for them. It can become material, but we're not there yet," Shenfeld added. The S&P 500 SPX is clinging to positive gains in 2026 and has returned 100% over the past four years.

Fed officials are focused on the risks to the economy and markets from a reversal of optimism surrounding AI. Minutes of their October meeting disclosed that officials had lengthy discussions over various scenarios surrounding a possible market selloff.

"They are starting to get serious about what their playbook would be if this would get worse," Anderson said. The biggest worry would be "systemic dislocation" in financial markets, he added.

That might require the Fed to set up special credit lines to inject liquidity into markets, similar to actions taken in the financial crisis of 2008 and the dawn of the COVID pandemic in 2020, Anderson said.

At the moment, the Fed might be breathing "a sigh of relief" over the recent stock-market drop because it is concerned about high stock valuations and related hedge-fund leverage. A modest decline in equities "lets some the air out of the balloon," Anderson said.

Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide Financial, said if the Fed skips a hike in December, they would be accused of putting a floor under stock prices - in other words, "a Fed put" - a charge that has dogged the central bank since the late 1980s.

How bad would the stock-market selloff does have to get before the Fed changes their thinking about interest rates?

Officials will keep an eye on bank distress and distress in the plumbing of financial markets as signs that there may be more trouble lurking, Anderson said.

For now, a hike in December is seen as a done deal given the hot October inflation readings. After that, the future direction of the Fed becomes more of an open question.

Concerns about financial conditions seem to favor a gradual pace of hikes, meaning the Fed pausing at its January meeting and hiking again in March, wrote Michael Gapen, chief U.S. economist at Morgan Stanley, in a note to clients.

Many economist have penciled in a more aggressive rate path, with the Fed hiking three times - in December, January and March, before pausing to assess conditions. Shenfeld said he expects two hikes, one next month and another in January.

"I think they are worried about inflation getting ingrained at 3% as opposed to 2%, which is why they are willing to put a bit of a dent into growth to pull inflation down," Shenfeld said.

A modest slowdown in growth coupled with lower oil prices could take a lot of the wind out of inflation, he added.

Some economists are worried that the Fed will overtighten, and are blinded by concern that they haven't hit their 2% inflation target in almost six years.

"Markets are signaling that the current level of interest rates is unsustainably high," wrote Andrew Hollenhorst, U.S. chief economist at Citi, who is one of the most dovish economists on Wall Street.

A rate hike remains likely early next month, but then the Fed will stay on hold and eventually cut later next year, he said in a note to clients.

-Greg Robb
